docs.title: What is coa-judicial-behavior?
docs.text:
Debates about judges reach for two labels, "liberal" and "conservative," and empirical research has mostly measured one dimension, ideology, often by no more than the party of the president who appointed a judge. A series of studies of the judges of the federal courts of appeals measured four traits from what judges actually do, and found that they are distinct: ideology, activism, partisanship, and independence. This project computes those four scores for every judge of the courts of appeals from the opinions on CourtListener, collected and coded with courtpy, and adds them (and the variables made from them) to every vote, for control and prediction.

Score Study What it measures Scale Ideology Corey Rayburn Yung, Judged by the Company You Keep: An Empirical Study of the Ideologies of Judges on the United States Courts of Appeals, 51 B.C. L. Rev. 1133 (2010) How much more often a judge agrees with judges appointed by Republican presidents (copanelists, and the district judges whose judgments the judge affirms) than with those appointed by Democratic presidents. -100 (liberal) to 100 (conservative) Activism Corey Rayburn Yung, Flexing Judicial Muscle: An Empirical Study of Judicial Activism in the Federal Courts, 105 Nw. U. L. Rev. 1 (2011) How much more often a judge reverses under deferential standards of review than the judge's own rate under de novo review would predict: failing to defer when the formal model of law says to. 0 to 100 Partisanship Corey Rayburn Yung, Beyond Ideology: An Empirical Study of Partisanship and Independence in the Federal Courts, 80 Geo. Wash. L. Rev. 505 (2012) Whether a judge applies a neutral rule (the standard of review) with more deference to district judges appointed by the judge's own party. 0 to 100 Independence Beyond Ideology (2012) How often a judge provokes dissents and separate concurrences beyond what the judge's ideological distance from the circuit predicts. 0 to 100

A Typology of Judging Styles, 107 Nw. U. L. Rev. 1757 (2013), revised all four together and sorted the judges into nine judging styles by Ward's cluster analysis of the scores: Trailblazing, Consensus Building, Stalwart, Regulating, Steadfast, Collegial, Incrementalist, Minimalist, and Error Correcting. This project follows the 2013 methods by default (method = "typology"), and each score's first article with method = "original".

docs.title: Why use coa-judicial-behavior?
docs.text:
• Faithful. Each score follows the formulas and adjustments of the articles: case mix, the "super-panel" of copanelists and district judge, circuit differences measured by judges who travel between circuits, and common scales. The tests reproduce the worked examples of the articles (such as Judge Diane Wood's Activism Differential).
  • Every opinion, every year. The studies hand-coded the 30,000 votes of 2008. CourtListener has the published and unpublished opinions of every year, and courtpy codes them by rules in spreadsheets, so the scores can be computed for any period (or each year separately) and replicated.
  • Ready to predict with. The scores, the panel's scores, and the interactions the articles tested (such as partisanship toward a district judge of the other party) are added to every vote, and the studies' probit tests are repeated on votes that the scores never saw.

docs.title: Methods
docs.text:
Each score starts from a table of votes, with one row for each judge on each case: whether the judge voted to reverse, dissented, or concurred; the standard of review ("deferential" for clear error, abuse of discretion, arbitrary and capricious, substantial evidence, or plain error; "non_deferential" for de novo review; "unclear" for both or neither); and the judge's super-panel: the two copanelists and the district judge, and the parties of the presidents who appointed them (such as "RR-D").

Score Raw score Ideology Panel Score: rate of agreement with Republican-appointed copanelists less the rate with Democratic-appointed ones. District Score: the same for affirmances of district judges, weighting each standard of review by the inverse of its rate of reversal. Activism Reversal rate under deferential standards less the reversal rate under de novo review. Partisanship (Deferential reversal rate of district judges of the other party less that of the judge's own party) less (the same under nondeferential review). Independence Rate of dissents plus rate of concurrences (the judge's own, and those against the judge's opinions) less the rates that a regression on the judge's distance from the circuit's mean ideology predicts.

Then every score is adjusted, as the articles adjusted them:

Adjustment How Case mix Each rate is computed for criminal and civil cases separately and weighted by the average judge's shares. Thin cells fall back on the judge's rate in both kinds of cases, then on all judges'. Super-panel effects The score that a blank-slate judge would have from the six alignments (RR-R, RR-D, DR-R, DR-D, DD-R, DD-D) that the judge happened to sit in is subtracted. Circuit Judges who sat in more than one circuit are assumed to keep their traits. Their pooled score in each circuit, less their vote-weighted overall scores, is the circuit's differential, which is subtracted per judge (2010, 2011) or per vote (2012, 2013). Scale The judges with at least 200 interactions (two copanelists and a district judge per vote) define the scales. Independence is put on a logarithmic scale first.

The advanced user guide gives every formula, the differences between the two methods, and the few places where the articles left a choice open and how this project made it.

docs.title: The data
docs.text:
courtpy extracts the opinions of the twelve regional circuits from CourtListener's bulk data and parses them with its federal rules, which find the judges of the panel, who wrote, joined, concurred, or dissented, the disposition, the parties, and four standards of review. This project's rules, in instructions/review.csv, add what the scores need:

Variable Meaning district_judges The district judge's name, from the lines about the court appealed from, in each circuit's form ("Catherine C. Blake, District Judge", "(Hon. Lewis A. Kaplan, Judge)", "District Judge: Honorable Joel A. Pisano", and others). review_district, review_agency Whether the appeal came from a district court, or is a petition to review an agency. review_immigration Immigration review, which the studies left out (as they left out habeas corpus). standard_substantial_evidence, standard_plain_error, standard_named Two deferential standards that courtpy does not find, and words that announce any standard of review.

The techniques (which importing the package adds to the amos library) then build the votes:

Technique Adds code_district_judge The district judge, found among the district judges of the case's circuit who were serving that year (district_judge, district_judge_nid), with the party of the appointing president (district_party) and Judicial Common Space score (district_jcs). code_review review_standard, review_deferential, review_de_novo, review_has_standard, review_excluded (habeas corpus and immigration), and review_of_district. review_votes courtpy's table of votes (one row for each judge on each case, with vote_reversal, judge_dissented, judge_concurred, judge_author, and each judge's attributes), with the super-panel: copanel, alignment, colleagues_republican, district_opposed, and panel_unanimous. score_judges The table of scores and the judging styles (see below), and the predictors on every vote. validate_scores The studies' tests of the scores.

The roster of judges comes from the Federal Judicial Center's biographical directory (through courtpy and fjc-biographies), with each appointment's Judicial Common Space score and the careers that the studies tested, coded by the rules in instructions/careers.csv: prosecutor, public defender, law clerk, law professor, Department of Justice, state judge, legislative and executive service, and others.

Two differences from the studies' data are worth knowing. The studies coded 2008 from LexisNexis, by hand and later partly by software, and their coders resolved which standard was actually applied when an opinion named several; here an opinion that names both kinds is "unclear." And some circuits do not name the district judge in their opinions (the Fifth Circuit's unpublished opinions often give only the district court's docket number); those votes count toward the Panel Score and independence, but not toward the scores that need the district judge.

docs.title: The variables
docs.text:
score_judges adds a table, "score_judges", with a row for each judge:

Column Meaning judge_nid, judge, judge_party, circuit The judge, the party of the appointing president (-1 or 1), and the judge's home circuit. votes, panel_interactions, district_interactions, interactions, traveling_votes, qualified How much the judge was observed, and whether the judge defines the scales (at least minimum interactions). ideology, activism, partisanship, independence The four scores. ideological is the absolute Ideology Score. ideology_panel, ideology_district, ideology_raw The Panel, District, and raw Ideology Scores. {score}_raw, {score}_super_panel, {score}_circuit, {score}_adjusted Each step of the adjustments, for ideology, activism, and partisanship. dissent_rate, concurrence_rate, expected_dissent_rate, expected_concurrence_rate, independence_raw, independence_log The steps of the Independence Score. cluster, style The judge's judging style.

And every vote gets these variables for control and prediction:

Variable Meaning judge_ideology, judge_ideological, judge_activism, judge_partisanship, judge_independence, judge_style, judge_scored The judge's scores and style, and whether the judge had enough interactions to define the scales. colleagues_{score} The mean score of the judge's copanelists. panel_ideology_median, panel_ideology_net The panel's median and summed Ideology Scores, the measures that the 2010 article tested. panel_activism_mean, panel_partisanship_mean, panel_independence_mean, panel_independence_max The panel's other scores. ideological_distance How far the judge's ideology is from the copanelists'. circuit_ideology, circuit_deviation The circuit's mean ideology, and how far the judge is from it (which predicts separate opinions). ideological_pressure The ideology (as -1 to 1) times the district judge's side: positive when a conservative judge reviews a Democratic appointee or a liberal judge a Republican one. partisan_pressure The centered Partisanship Score times 1 for a district judge of the other party and -1 for one of the same party. activist_pressure The centered Activism Score under a deferential standard (0 otherwise). expected_reversal The rate of reversal of all judges in the vote's alignment, case type, and standard: the super-panel effect itself. concurred_only Whether the judge concurred without dissenting. holdout Whether the vote was left out of the scores.

The controls that the articles used come with the votes: the case type, the standard of review, the circuit, the year, publication, the super-panel, and each judge's attributes from the roster (judge_party, judge_jcs, judge_woman, judge_minority, judge_age, judge_senior, judge_designated, and the careers, such as judge_law_professor and judge_justice_department).

docs.title: Judging styles
docs.text: score_judges sorts the judges who define the scales into styles by Ward's cluster analysis of the absolute Ideology Score and the Activism, Partisanship, and Independence Scores, as the 2013 article did, and names each cluster for the article's style whose profile its mean scores are closest to. The "typology" table gives each cluster's mean scores, in points and in standard deviations, and how far it is from its style's profile; "typology_differences" is the article's test that every pair of clusters differs by at least one standard deviation in some score. The names are a guide to reading the clusters: the clusters of other judges and years need not look like the article's.

docs.title: Testing the scores
docs.text:
validate_scores repeats the articles' tests, as probit regressions with standard errors clustered by case, on the votes left out of the scores:

Test Outcome Measures civil_rights (2010) Whether a plaintiff under Title VII, section 1983, or the ADA won The panel's median and net Ideology Scores, against its median Judicial Common Space score and the mean party of its appointing presidents. dissent, concurrence (2012) Whether the judge dissented or concurred The Independence Score, against the absolute Ideology and Judicial Common Space scores. partisan_reversal (2012) Whether the judge voted to reverse, under a deferential standard partisan_pressure, against ideological_pressure and the district judge's party alone. activist_reversal (2011) The same The Activism Score.

docs.title: Requirements
docs.text: The project requires Python 3.11 or later and uv. It runs on Linux, macOS, and Windows. The first run downloads CourtListener's bulk files of opinions, clusters, and dockets (about 63 GB, kept outside the project and reused) unless courtpy has already downloaded them, and the Federal Judicial Center's files of judges. No API key is needed.

docs.text:
In the project's folder:

uv sync

docs.title: Usage
docs.text:
Make the roster of judges once (with the careers and Judicial Common Space scores), and then run the study:

uv run coa-judicial-behavior judges
uv run coa-judicial-behavior run studies/judicial_behavior.toml --export

The study, studies/judicial_behavior.toml, scores the judges from the votes through 2020, tests the scores on the later votes, estimates a probit model of reversal with circuit and year fixed effects, and compares models that predict the later votes. Every choice is a setting there, such as method, minimum, the years scored, or by = "year" to score each year separately, as the studies scored 2008.

In Python:

import coa_judicial_behavior

project = coa_judicial_behavior.Project.create("studies/judicial_behavior.toml")
scores = project.result.tables["score_judges"]
print(scores[scores["qualified"]].sort_values("activism").tail(10))
print(project.result.tables["typology"])
print(project.result.tables["validate_scores"])

To score a table of votes that is already saved (one row for each judge on each case, as review_votes makes it):

import pandas as pd
import coa_judicial_behavior

votes = pd.read_parquet("votes.parquet")
scores = coa_judicial_behavior.score_judges(votes, method = "typology", by = "year")
styles = coa_judicial_behavior.classify(scores[scores["year"] == 2008])
predictors = coa_judicial_behavior.add_predictors(votes, scores, by = "year")

or from a terminal:

uv run coa-judicial-behavior scores votes.parquet --output results/judge_scores.csv --by year

Every other command is courtpy's (such as download, parse, and rules), with this project's techniques available.

docs.text: Path Holds studies/judicial_behavior.toml The settings of the study. src/coa_judicial_behavior/instructions/ The rules that find the district judge and the review (review.csv), and that code the judges' careers (careers.csv). src/coa_judicial_behavior/votes.py code_review, code_district_judge, and review_votes, which make the votes. src/coa_judicial_behavior/scores.py score_judges, the four scores. src/coa_judicial_behavior/typology.py classify, the judging styles. src/coa_judicial_behavior/predictions.py add_predictors, score_judges (the technique), and validate_scores. tests/ Tests, with fictional judges and cases, including a simulation of judges whose traits are known.

docs.title: Advanced User Guide
docs.text: This guide gives the formulas of the four scores as score_judges computes them, the differences between the methods of the articles, and the places where the articles left a choice open and how this project made it.

docs.title: Notation
docs.text:
For a judge, t is a case type (criminal or civil) and s a standard of review (deferential, nondeferential, or unclear). share(t) is the average judge's share of votes in criminal or civil cases (the mean over judges of each judge's share), which the articles called "the distribution of the average judge." Every rate is a judge's mean in a cell, such as the judge's rate of reversal in civil cases under deferential standards.

Thin cells. When a judge has fewer than cell_minimum votes (5 by default) in a cell, the judge's rate in that cell for criminal and civil cases together is used, and if that is thin too, the rate of all judges in the cell. The articles "interpolated based upon expected and actual scores with that judge's case mix"; this is one way to do that, and it never lets a single vote set a rate.

docs.title: Ideology
docs.text:
Panel Score = sum_t share(t) * (Agree(Rep, t) - Agree(Dem, t))

Agree(P, t) is the share of the judge's pairs with copanelists of party P in which the two agreed (both joined the majority, or both dissented).

District Score = sum_t share(t) * sum_s w(t, s) * (Affirm(Rep, t, s) - Affirm(Dem, t, s))

Affirm(P, t, s) is the judge's rate of affirming district judges of party P. The weight of a standard is

w(t, s) = W(t, s) * n(t, s) / sum_s' W(t, s') * n(t, s')
W(t, s) = (1 / ReversalRate(t, s)) / sum_s' (1 / ReversalRate(t, s'))

where n(t, s) is the judge's number of votes reviewing district judges in the cell and ReversalRate(t, s) the rate of all judges. In the 2010 article's example, the weights of criminal cases were 0.479 (deferential), 0.241 (nondeferential), and 0.280 (unclear), which is what inverse rates of reversal give. The article's expression divided the weighted sum by the total number of votes and then halved it "to keep the District Score on the same relative scale"; normalizing the weights within each case type does that exactly, for any mix of votes.

The raw score combines the two:

Method Raw Ideology Score original (2010) Panel Score + District Score typology (2013) (d_panel * Panel Score + d_district * District Score) / (d_panel + d_district), where d is the rate of disagreement at each level among all judges ("combined based upon the rate of disagreement at each level").

Zero and scale. The 2010 article put zero at the mean of the k-th and (k+1)-th most liberal judges, where k is the number of Democratic appointees, and scaled so that the judge farthest from zero is at -100 or 100. The 2013 article kept zero where it is (equal agreement with both parties) and chose "the multiplier ... that would either move the highest score to 100 or lowest score to [-]100."

docs.title: Activism
docs.text:
Activism Differential = sum_t share(t) * (Reversal(deferential, t) - Reversal(nondeferential, t))

Judge Wood's example in the 2011 article (4 reversals in 53 deferential votes and 13 in 49 de novo votes) is a test of this project. The article's case-mix expression estimated a judge's criminal and civil rates from the judge's totals and the average judge's distributions, because its data were thin; this project computes the rates in each case type directly, with the fallbacks above. Votes under an unclear standard do not count.

The 2011 article made no super-panel adjustment; the 2013 article did, and so does method = "typology".

docs.title: Partisanship
docs.text:
Partisanship = sum_t share(t) * ((DefRev(other, t) - DefRev(own, t)) - (NonRev(other, t) - NonRev(own, t)))

DefRev(other, t) is the judge's rate of reversing district judges appointed by the other party under deferential standards, and so on. This is the 2012 article's raw formula (with Democratic and Republican district judges) multiplied by the judge's own party (1 for a Republican appointee and -1 for a Democratic one), which is the article's "one unique alteration": a Democratic appointee who favors Republican district judges is not partisan. Writing it with "own" and "other" party lets the traveling judges of a circuit, who belong to both parties, be scored together.

docs.title: Independence
docs.text:
Independence = sum_t share(t) * (Dissents(t) + Concurrences(t) - E[Dissents(t)] - E[Concurrences(t)])

Dissents(t) is the judge's dissents per vote plus, by default, the dissents of copanelists against opinions that the judge wrote (provoked = "author", the 2012 article's "writes an opinion that draws a dissenting opinion"). provoked = "panel" counts dissents against any majority that the judge joined, which is how the 2013 article's footnote ("the difference between dissenting and being dissented against is simply how the third judge on the panel voted") can be read. A concurrence in part and dissent in part is a dissent only.

The expected rates are the fitted values of a linear regression, across the judges who define the scales, of each rate on the absolute distance between the judge's ideology and the mean ideology of the judges of the judge's circuit. The 2012 article used the scaled Ideology Score; the 2013 article used "the degree to which a judge's Raw Ideology Score differed from the mean of the circuit," which method = "typology" uses (the adjusted raw score, before scaling).

The raw scores are shifted so that the lowest is log_offset (0.01 by default), and their logarithm is scaled from 0 to 100. The articles placed the scores "on a logarithmic scale (to create a normal distribution)" without saying how they made them positive; the offset is that choice, and a smaller one spreads out the lowest scores.

docs.title: Adjustments
docs.text:
Super-panel effects. Each vote has an alignment: the parties of the two copanelists and of the district judge (RR-R, RR-D, DR-R, DR-D, DD-R, DD-D). For each alignment, case type, and standard, the rates of agreement and reversal of all judges are what a blank-slate judge would do there. The score is computed again with those rates in place of the judge's own, and that "expected" score is subtracted. So alignments that offset each other (thirty RR-R panels against ten DD-D panels, in the articles' example) cancel, and only the excess pulls the score, as the articles described.

Circuit. For each circuit, the votes there of judges who sat in more than one circuit are scored together as one hypothetical judge ("actual"), and compared with those judges' overall scores weighted by their votes there ("expected"). The differential, actual less expected, is subtracted:

circuit Amount subtracted from a judge's score Used by per_judge The differential of the judge's home circuit / (2 * the judges of the circuit) 2010 (ideology) and 2011 (activism) per_vote The sum over circuits of the differential / the traveling votes there * the judge's votes there 2012 (partisanship) and 2013 (all three) full The sum over circuits of the differential * the judge's share of votes there Not in the articles none Nothing Independence, in both

The per_vote formula follows the 2012 and 2013 appendices literally ("the raw adjustment number was then divided by the number of traveling votes in the circuit ... Then each judge within the circuit would have the circuit adjustment applied based upon the number of votes he or she issued"). When a circuit has few traveling votes and its judges many votes, it can be larger than the differential itself; the {score}_circuit column shows its size, and circuit = "full" is the alternative that never is.

Scale. The judges with at least minimum interactions (200 in the articles) define every scale. Activism, partisanship, and independence are shifted so that the lowest of them is 0 and multiplied so that the highest is 100; other judges can fall outside 0 to 100.

docs.title: Methods at a glance
docs.text: Choice method = "original" method = "typology" Raw Ideology Score Panel + District Weighted by the rates of disagreement Ideology's zero The k-th judge (k = Democratic appointees) Equal agreement with both parties Super-panel adjustment Ideology, partisanship Ideology, activism, partisanship Circuit adjustment Per judge (ideology, activism), per vote (partisanship) Per vote Independence's expected rates Scaled Ideology Score Adjusted raw Ideology Score

docs.title: Scoring periods
docs.text: The articles scored one year. by = "year" (or any column) scores each value separately, with its own context (shares, weights, alignments, travelers, and scale), so the scores of different years are each relative to their own judges. A judge needs minimum interactions within a period to define its scales, so with one year at a time a lower minimum may be needed in small circuits.

docs.title: Judging styles
docs.text: classify uses scipy's Ward linkage on the four scores (the absolute Ideology Score, which is from 0 to 100, and the other three), cuts the tree into clusters groups, and numbers them in the order of the tree's leaves. With nine clusters, each is matched to one of the article's styles by the smallest total squared distance between the clusters' standardized means and the styles' profiles (read from the article's descriptions in Part III.B: "high" is about one standard deviation, "highest" or "lowest" about one and a half). The "distance" column of the "typology" table says how well each cluster fits its style.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text: All notable changes to this project will be documented in this file.

• Created the repository from the snickerdoodle template.
  • Added the four scores of Corey Rayburn Yung's studies of the judges of the federal courts of appeals (score_judges): ideology (2010), activism (2011), partisanship and independence (2012), with the 2013 revisions (method = "typology", the default) or each score's first article (method = "original"), and their case-mix, super-panel, circuit, and scaling adjustments.
  • Added the judging styles of A Typology of Judging Styles (classify), by Ward's cluster analysis, with the article's test that the styles are distinct.
  • Added the variables for control and prediction (add_predictors) and the studies' probit tests of the scores (validate_scores), on votes left out of the scores.
  • Added rules that find the district judge, the origin of the appeal, immigration review, and two more deferential standards in CourtListener opinions (instructions/review.csv), and rules that code the judges' careers (instructions/careers.csv).
  • Added the techniques code_review, code_district_judge, and review_votes, the commands judges and scores, and the study studies/judicial_behavior.toml.

docs.title: Environment Setup
docs.text:
Install uv, then create a virtual environment with all of the development dependencies from the repository folder:

uv sync

Then, install the pre-commit hooks so that they run before each commit:

uv run pre-commit install

Run the tests with uv run pytest.

docs.title: Development
docs.text:
Follow this basic process:

  1. Fork and clone the repository.
  2. Create a new branch: git checkout -b feature-or-bugfix-name.
  3. Edit the code.
  4. If you added functionality or features, update the documentation accordingly.

If you are unsure about how to fix or ignore a warning, just let the continuous integration fail, and we will help you during review.

Don't bother updating the changelog, we will take care of this.

docs.title: Pull requests guidelines
docs.text:
Link to any related issue in the Pull Request message.

During the review, we recommend using fixups:

# SHA is the SHA of the commit you want to fix
git commit --fixup=SHA

Once all the changes are approved, you can squash your commits:

git rebase -i --autosquash main

And force-push:

git push -f

If this seems all too complicated, you can push or force-push each new commit, and we will squash them ourselves if needed, before merging.

docs.title: Style Guidelines
docs.text:
This package follows the Google Python Style Guide with two notable exceptions:

  1. It always adds spaces around "=". This not only violates the Google guide, it violates PEP8, the foundational Python style guide from which all other resources are derived. I defy this strong, long-standing norm because I find it more readable. My brain and eyes have trouble seeing two separate objects when an equal sign is in the middle. I imagine that I am not alone in this accessibility issue. Further, as PEP8 itself notes, required spaces around equal signs are becoming increasing common with type annotations becoming part of best practices (and, as a result, signatures to classes, functions, and methods regularly include spaces around the equal signs). I realize that this will seem alien to many coders, but it is far easier on my eyes.
  2. I use some so-called "power features", primarily dunder methods, to make my interfaces easier to access and use. This is disfavored in the Google Python Style Guide because such code is often more difficult for others to read. To address that concern, I try to document and comment as to what the code is doing whenever I used any of the "power features" of Python.

Because of the first exception, the project does not use a code formatter (such as ruff format), which would remove those spaces.

docs.title: Tutorial
docs.text: This tutorial computes the four scores for the judges of the federal courts of appeals, from the opinions on CourtListener to a table of scores.

docs.title: 1. Install
docs.text:
In the project's folder:

uv sync

docs.title: 2. Make the roster of judges
docs.text:
The roster identifies the judges of each panel and the district judges, with the party of the president who appointed each, their careers, and their Judicial Common Space scores. It downloads three small files from the Federal Judicial Center and the scores' sources, and saves the roster where courtpy looks for it:

uv run coa-judicial-behavior judges

docs.title: 3. Try the rules on a few cases
docs.text:
Before parsing every opinion, extract a few and check what the rules find:

uv run coa-judicial-behavior download bulk --courts ca4 --start 2019-01-01 --end 2019-01-31 --folder data/court_listener
uv run coa-judicial-behavior parse data/court_listener --rulebooks federal src/coa_judicial_behavior/instructions/review.csv --output data/sample.csv

In data/sample.csv, district_judges should name the district judge of most appeals from district courts, and the standard_... columns the standards of review.

docs.title: 4. Run the study
docs.text:
uv run coa-judicial-behavior run studies/judicial_behavior.toml --export

The first run extracts every opinion of the twelve regional circuits since 2008 (a few hours), parses and codes them, and saves the coded appeals in data/appeals.parquet, which later runs reuse. The results are exported to results/:

Table Holds score_judges A row for each judge: the four scores, each step of their adjustments, and the judging style. typology, typology_differences The judging styles and the article's test that they are distinct. validate_scores The studies' tests of the scores on votes after 2020. fixest_coefficients A probit model of reversal with circuit and year fixed effects. analyst_comparison, scorecard, permutation_importance How well models predict the votes after 2020, and which variables matter most.

docs.title: 5. Change the study
docs.text:
Every choice is a setting in studies/judicial_behavior.toml:

  • method = "original" follows each score's first article instead of the 2013 revision.
  • by = "year" scores each year separately, as the studies scored 2008 (with a lower minimum, such as 100, for small circuits).
  • train sets the votes that the scores come from, and so the votes they are tested on.
  • Add and court_num != 12 to the query of filter_rows to leave out the D.C. Circuit, as the studies did.

Delete data/appeals.parquet after changing the rules, the roster, or the loader's parameters, so that the opinions are parsed again.

docs.title: Index
docs.text:
Ideology, activism, partisanship, and independence of appellate judges.

The scores follow the methods of Corey Rayburn Yung's studies of the judges of the federal courts of appeals (see coa_judicial_behavior.scores), from opinions that courtpy collects from CourtListener and codes. Importing the package adds its techniques to the amos library, so a study's settings can name them: code_review, code_district_judge, review_votes, score_judges, and validate_scores.

Contents

CodeDistrictJudge: finds the district judge whose judgment each case reviews. CodeReview: sorts each case by its standard of review. PREDICTORS: the variables for control and prediction that the scores add to the votes. Project: amos.Project (which courtpy offers under the same name), which loads and analyzes the cases that a settings file describes. ReviewVotes: makes the table of votes, with each vote's super-panel. RULEBOOK: the path of the rules that find what the scores need in each opinion. ScoreJudges: scores the judges and adds the predictors to the votes. Typology: the judging styles of the judges. ValidateScores: repeats the studies' tests of the scores. add_predictors: adds the scores to a table of votes. classify: sorts judges into judging styles. score_judges: returns the four scores of every judge. validate: returns the studies' tests of the scores.

def munge(
    self,
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    roster: judges.Roster | pd.DataFrame | pathlib.Path | str | None = (
        None),
    column: str = 'district_judges',
    attributes: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Adds the district judge of each case.

    Args:
        data: the parsed cases.
        roster: a roster, the table of one, or the path of a saved one.
            Defaults to `None`, in which case the roster saved in
            "judges" in courtpy's data folder is used.
        column: name of the column with the names of the district judge.
            Defaults to "district_judges".
        attributes: names of the roster's columns to add, other than
            "party". Defaults to `None`, in which case "jcs" is added if
            the roster has it.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if the cases lack a column that is needed.

    Returns:
        The cases, with the new columns.

    """
    missing = [
        c for c in (column, 'court_num', 'year') if c not in data.columns]
    if missing:
        message = f'{self.name!r} needs the columns {missing}'
        raise KeyError(message)
    found = judges.Roster.create(roster)
    table = found.data
    if attributes is None:
        attributes = ['jcs'] if 'jcs' in table.columns else []
    wanted = ['party', *[
        a for a in _listify(attributes) if a in table.columns]]
    district = table[table['court_type'] == _DISTRICT_COURT]
    circuits = {
        int(float(str(number))): judges.Roster(rows, grace = found.grace)
        for number, rows in district.groupby('circuit_num')}
    panels = _panel_nids(data)
    rows: list[dict[str, Any]] = []
    for names, court, year, panel in zip(
        data[column], data['court_num'], data['year'], panels,
        strict = True):
        rows.append(_district_judge(
            _names(names), circuits.get(_whole(court) or -1),
            _whole(year), panel, wanted))
    added = pd.DataFrame(rows, index = data.index)
    data['district_judge'] = added['district_judge'].astype(object)
    data['district_judge_nid'] = added['district_judge_nid'].astype(
        'Int64')
    for name in wanted:
        data[f'district_{name}'] = added[name].astype('float64')
    return data

docs.text:
Bases: Munger

Sorts each case by its standard of review.

Standards of review are the formal rules that tell an appellate court how much to defer to the court below, and the activism, partisanship, and ideology scores all compare what judges do under deferential and nondeferential standards. A case is "deferential" if the opinion names only deferential standards (clear error, abuse of discretion, arbitrary and capricious, substantial evidence, or plain error), "non_deferential" if it names only de novo review, and "unclear" if it names both or neither, which is how the studies sorted them. Adds:

Column Meaning review_standard "deferential", "non_deferential", or "unclear". review_deferential, review_de_novo Whether the standard is deferential, or de novo. review_has_standard Whether the opinion names any standard of review (or uses words that announce one), as every case in the studies did. review_excluded Whether the case is one that the studies left out: habeas corpus or immigration. review_of_district Whether the case reviews a district court: the appeal came from one (or its judge was found), and it is not a petition to review an agency.

Needs the standard_... flags. Uses the columns that "instructions/review.csv" makes, and the habeas and immigration flags of courtpy's civil rules, if they exist.

def munge(
    self,
    data: pd.DataFrame,
    deferential: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    non_deferential: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    excluded: Sequence[str] | str | None = None,
    **kwargs: Any) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Sorts each case by its standard of review.

    Args:
        data: the parsed cases.
        deferential: names of the flags of deferential standards.
            Defaults to `None`, in which case they are `DEFERENTIAL`.
        non_deferential: names of the flags of nondeferential standards.
            Defaults to `None`, in which case they are `NON_DEFERENTIAL`.
        excluded: names of the flags of the cases to leave out. Defaults
            to `None`, in which case they are habeas corpus and
            immigration.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Raises:
        KeyError: if the cases have none of the flags of either kind of
            standard.

    Returns:
        The cases, with the new columns.

    """
    deferring = _any(data, _listify(deferential) or DEFERENTIAL)
    novo = _any(data, _listify(non_deferential) or NON_DEFERENTIAL)
    if deferring is None or novo is None:
        message = (
            f'{self.name!r} needs the flags of the standards of review '
            f'(such as "standard_de_novo"), which the federal rules of '
            f'courtpy make'
        )
        raise KeyError(message)
    standard = np.select(
        [deferring & ~novo, novo & ~deferring],
        ['deferential', 'non_deferential'], default = 'unclear')
    data['review_standard'] = pd.Series(
        standard, index = data.index, dtype = object)
    data['review_deferential'] = data['review_standard'] == 'deferential'
    data['review_de_novo'] = data['review_standard'] == 'non_deferential'
    named = _any(data, ['standard_named'])
    data['review_has_standard'] = (
        deferring | novo | (False if named is None else named))
    left_out = _any(data, _listify(excluded) or _EXCLUDED)
    data['review_excluded'] = (
        pd.Series(False, index = data.index) if left_out is None
        else left_out)
    district = _any(data, ['review_district'])
    agency = _any(data, ['review_agency'])
    found = (
        data['district_judge_nid'].notna()
        if 'district_judge_nid' in data.columns else False)
    data['review_of_district'] = (
        (pd.Series(False, index = data.index) if district is None
         else district) | found) & ~(
            False if agency is None else agency)
    return data

def apply(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    *,
    train: str | None = None,
    method: str = 'typology',
    minimum: int = 200,
    cell_minimum: int = 5,
    provoked: str = 'author',
    circuit: str | None = None,
    log_offset: float = 0.01,
    by: str | None = None,
    clusters: int = 9,
    styles: bool = True,
    merge: bool = True,
    **kwargs: Any) -> amos.Dataset:
    """Scores the judges of the votes in `item`.

    Args:
        item: the dataset of votes (as `review_votes` makes it).
        train: a query that selects the votes to score from. Defaults to
            `None`, in which case every vote is used.
        method: "typology" or "original". Defaults to "typology".
        minimum: fewest interactions for a judge to define the scales.
            Defaults to 200.
        cell_minimum: fewest votes in a cell for a judge's own rate.
            Defaults to 5.
        provoked: "author" or "panel". Defaults to "author".
        circuit: the circuit adjustment, or `None` for each score's own
            under `method`. Defaults to `None`.
        log_offset: what is added before the logarithm of the raw
            Independence Scores. Defaults to 0.01.
        by: name of a column whose values are scored separately.
            Defaults to `None`.
        clusters: the number of judging styles. Defaults to 9.
        styles: whether to sort the judges into styles. Defaults to
            `True`.
        merge: whether to add the predictors to the votes. Defaults to
            `True`.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        The dataset, with the tables of scores and styles and, with
            `merge`, the predictors.

    """
    data = item.data
    mask = _selected(data, train)
    table = scoring.score_judges(
        data[mask], method = method, minimum = int(minimum),
        cell_minimum = int(cell_minimum), provoked = provoked,
        circuit = circuit, log_offset = float(log_offset), by = by)
    made = [self.name]
    if _flag(styles):
        table = _classify(table, int(clusters), by, item, made)
    item.tables[self.name] = table
    created: list[str] = []
    if _flag(merge):
        added = add_predictors(data, table, by = by, train = mask)
        added['holdout'] = ~mask.to_numpy()
        created = [c for c in added.columns if c not in data.columns]
        item.replace(added)
    item.record(
        self.name, tables = made, created = created,
        judges = len(table),
        qualified = int(table['qualified'].sum()),
        scored_votes = int(mask.sum()))
    return item

def add_predictors(
    votes: pd.DataFrame,
    scores: pd.DataFrame,
    *,
    by: str | None = None,
    train: pd.Series | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Adds the judges' scores and the variables made from them to the votes.

    Args:
        votes: a table of votes (see `review_votes`).
        scores: the table of scores (see `score_judges`), with "style" if the
            judges were sorted into styles.
        by: name of the column that the judges were scored separately by, if
            they were. Defaults to `None`.
        train: whether each vote was one that the scores were computed from,
            for "expected_reversal". Defaults to `None`, in which case every
            vote was.

    Returns:
        The votes, with the variables of `PREDICTORS` (except "holdout").

    """
    keys = ['judge_nid', *([by] if by else [])]
    columns = {
        score: f'judge_{score}' for score in _SCORES if score in scores}
    if 'style' in scores.columns:
        columns['style'] = 'judge_style'
    columns['qualified'] = 'judge_scored'
    judged = scores[[*keys, 'circuit', *columns]].rename(columns = columns)
    circuit = (
        judged[judged['judge_scored']]
        .groupby([*([by] if by else []), 'circuit'])['judge_ideology'].mean()
        .rename('circuit_ideology').reset_index())
    judged = judged.merge(circuit, on = [*([by] if by else []), 'circuit'],
                          how = 'left').drop(columns = 'circuit')
    table = votes.drop(
        columns = [c for c in judged.columns if c in votes.columns
                   and c not in keys] + [
            c for c in PREDICTORS if c in votes.columns and c != 'holdout'])
    numbers = pd.to_numeric(table['judge_nid'], errors = 'coerce')
    left = table.assign(judge_nid = numbers.astype('Int64'))
    judged = judged.assign(
        judge_nid = pd.to_numeric(judged['judge_nid']).astype('Int64'))
    merged = left.reset_index().merge(judged, on = keys, how = 'left')
    merged = merged.set_index(votes.index.name or 'index')
    merged.index.name = votes.index.name
    merged['judge_nid'] = votes['judge_nid'].to_numpy()
    merged['judge_scored'] = merged['judge_scored'].fillna(False).astype(bool)
    cases = merged['case_id']
    for score in _SCORES:
        column = f'judge_{score}'
        if column not in merged.columns:
            continue
        values = merged[column].astype('float64')
        total = values.groupby(cases).transform('sum')
        count = values.groupby(cases).transform('count')
        others = count - values.notna()
        merged[f'colleagues_{score}'] = (
            (total - values.fillna(0)) / others).where(others > 0)
    ideology = merged['judge_ideology'].astype('float64')
    merged['panel_ideology_median'] = ideology.groupby(cases).transform(
        'median')
    merged['panel_ideology_net'] = ideology.groupby(cases).transform(
        lambda v: v.sum(min_count = 1))
    for score in ('activism', 'partisanship', 'independence'):
        merged[f'panel_{score}_mean'] = merged[f'judge_{score}'].astype(
            'float64').groupby(cases).transform('mean')
    merged['panel_independence_max'] = merged['judge_independence'].astype(
        'float64').groupby(cases).transform('max')
    merged['ideological_distance'] = (
        ideology - merged['colleagues_ideology']).abs()
    merged['circuit_deviation'] = (ideology - merged['circuit_ideology']).abs()
    district = (
        pd.to_numeric(merged['district_party'], errors = 'coerce')
        if 'district_party' in merged.columns
        else pd.Series(np.nan, index = merged.index))
    merged['ideological_pressure'] = ideology / 100 * -district
    opposed = merged.get('district_opposed')
    side = (
        pd.Series(np.nan, index = merged.index) if opposed is None
        else pd.Series(np.where(
            opposed.astype('boolean').fillna(False), 1.0, -1.0),
            index = merged.index).where(opposed.notna()))
    merged['partisan_pressure'] = (
        (merged['judge_partisanship'] - 50) / 50 * side)
    deferential = (
        merged['review_deferential'].astype('boolean').fillna(False)
        if 'review_deferential' in merged.columns
        else merged['review_standard'] == 'deferential')
    merged['activist_pressure'] = (
        (merged['judge_activism'] - 50) / 50 * deferential.astype(float))
    merged['expected_reversal'] = _expected_reversal(merged, train)
    merged['concurred_only'] = (
        merged['judge_concurred'].astype('boolean').fillna(False)
        & ~merged['judge_dissented'].astype('boolean').fillna(False)).astype(
            bool)
    return merged

def classify(
    scores: pd.DataFrame,
    clusters: int = 9,
    *,
    names: Sequence[str] | None = None,
    only_qualified: bool = True) -> Typology:
    """Sorts judges into styles by Ward's cluster analysis.

    Args:
        scores: the table of scores (see `score_judges`), with "ideology",
            "activism", "partisanship", and "independence" (and "qualified",
            if `only_qualified`).
        clusters: the number of clusters. Defaults to 9, as in the article.
        names: the names of the styles to match the clusters to. Defaults to
            `None`, in which case they are `STYLES` if `clusters` is 9, and
            else the clusters are named by their numbers.
        only_qualified: whether to classify only the judges who define the
            scales of the scores. Defaults to `True`.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if there are fewer judges to classify than clusters.

    Returns:
        The styles of the judges.

    """
    features = pd.DataFrame({
        'ideological': scores['ideology'].abs(),
        'activism': scores['activism'],
        'partisanship': scores['partisanship'],
        'independence': scores['independence']}, index = scores.index)
    keep = features.notna().all(axis = 1)
    if only_qualified and 'qualified' in scores.columns:
        keep &= scores['qualified'].astype(bool)
    features = features[keep]
    if len(features) < max(clusters, 2):
        message = (
            f'{len(features)} judges cannot be sorted into {clusters} '
            f'clusters')
        raise ValueError(message)
    tree = hierarchy.linkage(features.to_numpy(dtype = 'float64'), 'ward')
    found = hierarchy.fcluster(tree, t = clusters, criterion = 'maxclust')
    # The clusters are numbered in the order that their judges first appear
    # among the leaves of the tree.
    leaves = hierarchy.leaves_list(tree)
    order: dict[int, int] = {}
    for leaf in leaves:
        order.setdefault(int(found[leaf]), len(order) + 1)
    numbered = pd.Series(
        [order[int(c)] for c in found], index = features.index,
        name = 'cluster')
    means = features.groupby(numbered).mean()
    spread = features.std(ddof = 1).replace(0, np.nan)
    standardized = (means - features.mean()) / spread
    labels, distance = _name(
        standardized, list(names) if names is not None else (
            list(STYLES) if len(means) == len(STYLES) else None))
    profiles = pd.concat([
        pd.DataFrame({
            'style': labels, 'judges': numbered.value_counts().sort_index()}),
        means,
        standardized.add_suffix('_z'),
        pd.DataFrame({'distance': distance})], axis = 1)
    profiles.index.name = 'cluster'
    gaps = means.to_numpy()[:, None, :] - means.to_numpy()[None, :, :]
    counts = (np.abs(gaps) >= spread.to_numpy()).sum(axis = 2)
    differences = pd.DataFrame(counts, index = means.index, columns = means.index)
    assignments = pd.DataFrame({
        'cluster': numbered, 'style': numbered.map(labels)})
    return Typology(
        assignments = assignments, profiles = profiles,
        differences = differences)

def score_judges(
    votes: pd.DataFrame,
    *,
    method: str = 'typology',
    minimum: int = 200,
    cell_minimum: int = 5,
    provoked: str = 'author',
    circuit: str | None = None,
    log_offset: float = 0.01,
    by: str | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the four scores of every judge in a table of votes.

    Args:
        votes: a table of votes, with one row for each judge on each case,
            as `review_votes` makes it. It needs "case_id", "judge_nid",
            "judge_party", "court_num", "type_criminal", "review_standard",
            "vote_reversal", "judge_dissented", "judge_concurred",
            "judge_author", "district_party", and "alignment". "judge" and
            "judge_designated" are used if they are there.
        method: "typology" (the 2013 article's methods) or "original" (each
            score's first article). Defaults to "typology".
        minimum: fewest interactions with other judges for a judge to define
            the scales. Defaults to 200, as in the studies.
        cell_minimum: fewest votes in a cell (such as criminal cases under a
            deferential standard) for the judge's own rate in it to be used.
            Defaults to 5.
        provoked: whose separate opinions count toward a judge's
            independence besides the judge's own: "author" (those against
            the opinion that the judge wrote, as the 2012 article describes)
            or "panel" (those against any majority that the judge joined).
            Defaults to "author".
        circuit: the circuit adjustment of ideology, activism, and
            partisanship: "per_judge", "per_vote", "full", or "none".
            Defaults to `None`, in which case each score's adjustment under
            `method` is used.
        log_offset: what is added to the shifted raw Independence Scores
            before their logarithm is taken, so that the lowest is not zero.
            Defaults to 0.01 (one percentage point).
        by: name of a column (such as "year") whose values are scored
            separately, as the studies scored one year. Defaults to `None`,
            in which case every vote is scored together.

    Raises:
        ValueError: if `method`, `provoked`, or `circuit` is not one of its
            choices.
        KeyError: if `votes` lacks a column that is needed.

    Returns:
        A table with a row for each judge (and value of `by`), sorted from
            the most liberal Ideology Score. Its columns are described in the
            documentation of the project.

    """
    _check(method, METHODS, 'method')
    _check(provoked, _PROVOKED, 'provoked')
    if circuit is not None:
        _check(circuit, _CIRCUIT_METHODS, 'circuit')

    def score(frame: pd.DataFrame) -> pd.DataFrame:
        return _score(
            frame, method = method, minimum = int(minimum),
            cell_minimum = int(cell_minimum), provoked = provoked,
            circuit = circuit, log_offset = float(log_offset))

    if by is None:
        return score(votes)
    tables = []
    for value, group in votes.groupby(by, sort = True):
        table = score(group)
        table.insert(1, by, value)
        tables.append(table)
    return pd.concat(tables, ignore_index = True)

def validate(
    votes: pd.DataFrame,
    *,
    holdout_only: bool = True,
    tests: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the studies' tests of the scores.

    | Test | Rows | Outcome | Measures |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | `civil_rights` | Cases under Title VII, section 1983, or the ADA whose plaintiff won or lost (2010) | `outcome_civil_plaintiff_won` | The panel's median and net Ideology Scores, its median Judicial Common Space score, and the mean party of its appointing presidents. |
    | `dissent` | Every vote (2012) | `judge_dissented` | The Independence Score, the absolute Ideology Score, and the absolute Judicial Common Space score. |
    | `concurrence` | Every vote (2012) | `concurred_only` | The same. |
    | `partisan_reversal` | Votes under a deferential standard with a district judge of known party (2012) | `vote_reversal` | `partisan_pressure`, `ideological_pressure`, and whether the district judge is of the other party. |
    | `activist_reversal` | Votes under a deferential standard (2011) | `vote_reversal` | The Activism Score. |

    Args:
        votes: the votes, with the predictors (see `add_predictors`).
        holdout_only: whether to test only the votes left out of the scores
            (if "holdout" is a column). Defaults to `True`.
        tests: names of the tests to run. Defaults to `None`, in which case
            every test whose columns exist is run.

    Returns:
        A table with a row for each test and measure: "test", "measure",
            "coefficient", "std_error", "z", "p_value", "pseudo_r2"
            (McFadden's), and "observations". A measure that could not be
            fitted (too few rows or no variation) has missing values.

    """
    data = votes
    if holdout_only and 'holdout' in data.columns and data['holdout'].any():
        data = data[data['holdout'].astype(bool)]
    deferential = (
        data['review_standard'] == 'deferential'
        if 'review_standard' in data.columns
        else pd.Series(False, index = data.index))
    data = data.assign(
        abs_jcs = pd.to_numeric(data['judge_jcs'], errors = 'coerce').abs()
        if 'judge_jcs' in data.columns else np.nan,
        district_other_party = pd.to_numeric(
            data['district_opposed'].astype('Float64'), errors = 'coerce')
        if 'district_opposed' in data.columns else np.nan)
    plans: dict[str, tuple[pd.DataFrame, str, list[str]]] = {}
    present = [c for c in _CIVIL_RIGHTS if c in data.columns]
    if present and 'outcome_civil_plaintiff_won' in data.columns:
        civil = data[data[present].fillna(False).astype(bool).any(axis = 1)]
        if 'judge_jcs' in civil.columns:
            civil = civil.assign(panel_jcs_median = pd.to_numeric(
                civil['judge_jcs'], errors = 'coerce').groupby(
                    civil['case_id']).transform('median'))
        civil = civil.drop_duplicates('case_id')
        plans['civil_rights'] = (
            civil, 'outcome_civil_plaintiff_won',
            ['panel_ideology_median', 'panel_ideology_net',
             'panel_jcs_median', 'panel_party'])
    plans['dissent'] = (
        data, 'judge_dissented',
        ['judge_independence', 'judge_ideological', 'abs_jcs'])
    plans['concurrence'] = (
        data, 'concurred_only',
        ['judge_independence', 'judge_ideological', 'abs_jcs'])
    plans['partisan_reversal'] = (
        data[deferential & data['district_other_party'].notna()],
        'vote_reversal',
        ['partisan_pressure', 'ideological_pressure', 'district_other_party'])
    plans['activist_reversal'] = (
        data[deferential], 'vote_reversal', ['judge_activism'])
    rows = []
    for test, (rows_of, outcome, measures) in plans.items():
        if tests is not None and test not in tests:
            continue
        if outcome not in rows_of.columns:
            continue
        for measure in measures:
            if measure not in rows_of.columns:
                continue
            rows.append({
                'test': test, 'measure': measure,
                **_probit(rows_of, outcome, measure)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns = [
        'test', 'measure', 'coefficient', 'std_error', 'z', 'p_value',
        'pseudo_r2', 'observations'])

docs.title: predictions
docs.text:
Adds the scores to the votes as variables for control and prediction.

The studies used the scores in two ways: to describe judges, and to predict what panels and judges do. The 2010 article predicted whether civil rights plaintiffs won from the panel's net and median Ideology Scores, the 2012 article predicted dissents and separate concurrences from the Independence Scores and partisan reversals from the Partisanship Scores, and each compared the scores with the measures they were meant to improve on (the party of the appointing president and the Judicial Common Space score). Each kept the votes that it predicted out of the scores, so that the scores would not predict the data they came from.

add_predictors adds each judge's scores, and those of the judge's panel, to every vote, with the variables that the studies controlled for or predicted with. Two techniques, which are added to the amos library as soon as coa_judicial_behavior is imported, use it:

  • score_judges (an amos.Operation) scores the judges from the votes that its "train" query selects (all of them, unless one is set), sorts them into judging styles, adds the tables of scores and styles to the dataset, and adds the predictors to every vote. "holdout" marks the votes that the scores were not computed from, which a study can then predict (with the "time_split" or "group_split" of amos, or by filtering).
  • validate_scores (an amos.Describer) repeats the studies' tests: probit regressions of each outcome on each measure, among the held-out votes.
Contents

Predictors

the variables that add_predictors adds, with what each means. ScoreJudges: scores the judges and adds the predictors to the votes. ValidateScores: repeats the studies' tests of the scores. add_predictors: adds the judges' scores and the variables made from them to a table of votes. validate: returns the studies' tests of the scores.

def apply(
    self,
    item: amos.Dataset,
    *,
    train: str | None = None,
    method: str = 'typology',
    minimum: int = 200,
    cell_minimum: int = 5,
    provoked: str = 'author',
    circuit: str | None = None,
    log_offset: float = 0.01,
    by: str | None = None,
    clusters: int = 9,
    styles: bool = True,
    merge: bool = True,
    **kwargs: Any) -> amos.Dataset:
    """Scores the judges of the votes in `item`.

    Args:
        item: the dataset of votes (as `review_votes` makes it).
        train: a query that selects the votes to score from. Defaults to
            `None`, in which case every vote is used.
        method: "typology" or "original". Defaults to "typology".
        minimum: fewest interactions for a judge to define the scales.
            Defaults to 200.
        cell_minimum: fewest votes in a cell for a judge's own rate.
            Defaults to 5.
        provoked: "author" or "panel". Defaults to "author".
        circuit: the circuit adjustment, or `None` for each score's own
            under `method`. Defaults to `None`.
        log_offset: what is added before the logarithm of the raw
            Independence Scores. Defaults to 0.01.
        by: name of a column whose values are scored separately.
            Defaults to `None`.
        clusters: the number of judging styles. Defaults to 9.
        styles: whether to sort the judges into styles. Defaults to
            `True`.
        merge: whether to add the predictors to the votes. Defaults to
            `True`.
        **kwargs: not used.

    Returns:
        The dataset, with the tables of scores and styles and, with
            `merge`, the predictors.

    """
    data = item.data
    mask = _selected(data, train)
    table = scoring.score_judges(
        data[mask], method = method, minimum = int(minimum),
        cell_minimum = int(cell_minimum), provoked = provoked,
        circuit = circuit, log_offset = float(log_offset), by = by)
    made = [self.name]
    if _flag(styles):
        table = _classify(table, int(clusters), by, item, made)
    item.tables[self.name] = table
    created: list[str] = []
    if _flag(merge):
        added = add_predictors(data, table, by = by, train = mask)
        added['holdout'] = ~mask.to_numpy()
        created = [c for c in added.columns if c not in data.columns]
        item.replace(added)
    item.record(
        self.name, tables = made, created = created,
        judges = len(table),
        qualified = int(table['qualified'].sum()),
        scored_votes = int(mask.sum()))
    return item

    votes: pd.DataFrame,
    scores: pd.DataFrame,
    *,
    by: str | None = None,
    train: pd.Series | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Adds the judges' scores and the variables made from them to the votes.

    Args:
        votes: a table of votes (see `review_votes`).
        scores: the table of scores (see `score_judges`), with "style" if the
            judges were sorted into styles.
        by: name of the column that the judges were scored separately by, if
            they were. Defaults to `None`.
        train: whether each vote was one that the scores were computed from,
            for "expected_reversal". Defaults to `None`, in which case every
            vote was.

    Returns:
        The votes, with the variables of `PREDICTORS` (except "holdout").

    """
    keys = ['judge_nid', *([by] if by else [])]
    columns = {
        score: f'judge_{score}' for score in _SCORES if score in scores}
    if 'style' in scores.columns:
        columns['style'] = 'judge_style'
    columns['qualified'] = 'judge_scored'
    judged = scores[[*keys, 'circuit', *columns]].rename(columns = columns)
    circuit = (
        judged[judged['judge_scored']]
        .groupby([*([by] if by else []), 'circuit'])['judge_ideology'].mean()
        .rename('circuit_ideology').reset_index())
    judged = judged.merge(circuit, on = [*([by] if by else []), 'circuit'],
                          how = 'left').drop(columns = 'circuit')
    table = votes.drop(
        columns = [c for c in judged.columns if c in votes.columns
                   and c not in keys] + [
            c for c in PREDICTORS if c in votes.columns and c != 'holdout'])
    numbers = pd.to_numeric(table['judge_nid'], errors = 'coerce')
    left = table.assign(judge_nid = numbers.astype('Int64'))
    judged = judged.assign(
        judge_nid = pd.to_numeric(judged['judge_nid']).astype('Int64'))
    merged = left.reset_index().merge(judged, on = keys, how = 'left')
    merged = merged.set_index(votes.index.name or 'index')
    merged.index.name = votes.index.name
    merged['judge_nid'] = votes['judge_nid'].to_numpy()
    merged['judge_scored'] = merged['judge_scored'].fillna(False).astype(bool)
    cases = merged['case_id']
    for score in _SCORES:
        column = f'judge_{score}'
        if column not in merged.columns:
            continue
        values = merged[column].astype('float64')
        total = values.groupby(cases).transform('sum')
        count = values.groupby(cases).transform('count')
        others = count - values.notna()
        merged[f'colleagues_{score}'] = (
            (total - values.fillna(0)) / others).where(others > 0)
    ideology = merged['judge_ideology'].astype('float64')
    merged['panel_ideology_median'] = ideology.groupby(cases).transform(
        'median')
    merged['panel_ideology_net'] = ideology.groupby(cases).transform(
        lambda v: v.sum(min_count = 1))
    for score in ('activism', 'partisanship', 'independence'):
        merged[f'panel_{score}_mean'] = merged[f'judge_{score}'].astype(
            'float64').groupby(cases).transform('mean')
    merged['panel_independence_max'] = merged['judge_independence'].astype(
        'float64').groupby(cases).transform('max')
    merged['ideological_distance'] = (
        ideology - merged['colleagues_ideology']).abs()
    merged['circuit_deviation'] = (ideology - merged['circuit_ideology']).abs()
    district = (
        pd.to_numeric(merged['district_party'], errors = 'coerce')
        if 'district_party' in merged.columns
        else pd.Series(np.nan, index = merged.index))
    merged['ideological_pressure'] = ideology / 100 * -district
    opposed = merged.get('district_opposed')
    side = (
        pd.Series(np.nan, index = merged.index) if opposed is None
        else pd.Series(np.where(
            opposed.astype('boolean').fillna(False), 1.0, -1.0),
            index = merged.index).where(opposed.notna()))
    merged['partisan_pressure'] = (
        (merged['judge_partisanship'] - 50) / 50 * side)
    deferential = (
        merged['review_deferential'].astype('boolean').fillna(False)
        if 'review_deferential' in merged.columns
        else merged['review_standard'] == 'deferential')
    merged['activist_pressure'] = (
        (merged['judge_activism'] - 50) / 50 * deferential.astype(float))
    merged['expected_reversal'] = _expected_reversal(merged, train)
    merged['concurred_only'] = (
        merged['judge_concurred'].astype('boolean').fillna(False)
        & ~merged['judge_dissented'].astype('boolean').fillna(False)).astype(
            bool)
    return merged

def validate(
    votes: pd.DataFrame,
    *,
    holdout_only: bool = True,
    tests: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> pd.DataFrame:
    """Returns the studies' tests of the scores.

    | Test | Rows | Outcome | Measures |
    | --- | --- | --- | --- |
    | `civil_rights` | Cases under Title VII, section 1983, or the ADA whose plaintiff won or lost (2010) | `outcome_civil_plaintiff_won` | The panel's median and net Ideology Scores, its median Judicial Common Space score, and the mean party of its appointing presidents. |
    | `dissent` | Every vote (2012) | `judge_dissented` | The Independence Score, the absolute Ideology Score, and the absolute Judicial Common Space score. |
    | `concurrence` | Every vote (2012) | `concurred_only` | The same. |
    | `partisan_reversal` | Votes under a deferential standard with a district judge of known party (2012) | `vote_reversal` | `partisan_pressure`, `ideological_pressure`, and whether the district judge is of the other party. |
    | `activist_reversal` | Votes under a deferential standard (2011) | `vote_reversal` | The Activism Score. |

    Args:
        votes: the votes, with the predictors (see `add_predictors`).
        holdout_only: whether to test only the votes left out of the scores
            (if "holdout" is a column). Defaults to `True`.
        tests: names of the tests to run. Defaults to `None`, in which case
            every test whose columns exist is run.

    Returns:
        A table with a row for each test and measure: "test", "measure",
            "coefficient", "std_error", "z", "p_value", "pseudo_r2"
            (McFadden's), and "observations". A measure that could not be
            fitted (too few rows or no variation) has missing values.

    """
    data = votes
    if holdout_only and 'holdout' in data.columns and data['holdout'].any():
        data = data[data['holdout'].astype(bool)]
    deferential = (
        data['review_standard'] == 'deferential'
        if 'review_standard' in data.columns
        else pd.Series(False, index = data.index))
    data = data.assign(
        abs_jcs = pd.to_numeric(data['judge_jcs'], errors = 'coerce').abs()
        if 'judge_jcs' in data.columns else np.nan,
        district_other_party = pd.to_numeric(
            data['district_opposed'].astype('Float64'), errors = 'coerce')
        if 'district_opposed' in data.columns else np.nan)
    plans: dict[str, tuple[pd.DataFrame, str, list[str]]] = {}
    present = [c for c in _CIVIL_RIGHTS if c in data.columns]
    if present and 'outcome_civil_plaintiff_won' in data.columns:
        civil = data[data[present].fillna(False).astype(bool).any(axis = 1)]
        if 'judge_jcs' in civil.columns:
            civil = civil.assign(panel_jcs_median = pd.to_numeric(
                civil['judge_jcs'], errors = 'coerce').groupby(
                    civil['case_id']).transform('median'))
        civil = civil.drop_duplicates('case_id')
        plans['civil_rights'] = (
            civil, 'outcome_civil_plaintiff_won',
            ['panel_ideology_median', 'panel_ideology_net',
             'panel_jcs_median', 'panel_party'])
    plans['dissent'] = (
        data, 'judge_dissented',
        ['judge_independence', 'judge_ideological', 'abs_jcs'])
    plans['concurrence'] = (
        data, 'concurred_only',
        ['judge_independence', 'judge_ideological', 'abs_jcs'])
    plans['partisan_reversal'] = (
        data[deferential & data['district_other_party'].notna()],
        'vote_reversal',
        ['partisan_pressure', 'ideological_pressure', 'district_other_party'])
    plans['activist_reversal'] = (
        data[deferential], 'vote_reversal', ['judge_activism'])
    rows = []
    for test, (rows_of, outcome, measures) in plans.items():
        if tests is not None and test not in tests:
            continue
        if outcome not in rows_of.columns:
            continue
        for measure in measures:
            if measure not in rows_of.columns:
                continue
            rows.append({
                'test': test, 'measure': measure,
                **_probit(rows_of, outcome, measure)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns = [
        'test', 'measure', 'coefficient', 'std_error', 'z', 'p_value',
        'pseudo_r2', 'observations'])

docs.text:
Scores the ideology, activism, partisanship, and independence of judges.

The four scores follow the methods of Corey Rayburn Yung's studies of the judges of the federal courts of appeals:

  • Ideology: Judged by the Company You Keep: An Empirical Study of the Ideologies of Judges on the United States Courts of Appeals, 51 B.C. L. Rev. 1133 (2010).
  • Activism: Flexing Judicial Muscle: An Empirical Study of Judicial Activism in the Federal Courts, 105 Nw. U. L. Rev. 1 (2011).
  • Partisanship and independence: Beyond Ideology: An Empirical Study of Partisanship and Independence in the Federal Courts, 80 Geo. Wash. L. Rev. 505 (2012).
  • All four, revised together: A Typology of Judging Styles, 107 Nw. U. L. Rev. 1757 (2013).

Each score is computed from a table of votes, with one row for each judge on each case (see coa_judicial_behavior.votes), in three steps: a raw score from rates of agreement and reversal, adjustments for what the judge could not choose (the mix of criminal and civil cases, the parties of the other judges of the "super-panel", and the circuit), and a common scale.

Ideology is an "agnostic" measure: judges who think alike vote together. Every judge is first given the party of the president who appointed the judge (-1 for a Democrat and 1 for a Republican), and the judge being scored is a blank slate. The Panel Score is the judge's rate of agreement with copanelists appointed by Republicans less the rate with those appointed by Democrats, and the District Score is the same for the district judges whose judgments the judge affirmed (an affirmance is an agreement and a reversal a disagreement). The District Score weights each standard of review by how rarely judgments are reversed under it, since affirming under a deferential standard says less about a judge than reversing under one:

Panel Score = sum over case types t of
    share(t) * (RateAgree(Rep, t) - RateAgree(Dem, t))
District Score = sum over t of share(t) * sum over standards s of
    w(t, s) * (RateAffirm(Rep, t, s) - RateAffirm(Dem, t, s))

where share(t) is the average judge's share of criminal or civil cases and w(t, s) is proportional to the judge's votes under each standard times the inverse of the rate of reversal under it (normalized to sum to one within each case type, which keeps the District Score on the scale of the Panel Score, as the 2010 article sought by halving its sum).

Activism is the difference between how often a judge reversed under deferential standards of review and under de novo review. The de novo rate is the baseline that removes reversals for ideological or other reasons, so what is left is how often the judge failed to defer when the formal model of law says that the judge should have:

Activism Differential = sum over t of share(t) *
    (ReversalRate(deferential, t) - ReversalRate(de novo, t))

Partisanship is whether a judge applied the same neutral rule (the standard of review) differently to district judges appointed by the two parties. It is signed by the judge's own party, so that a Democratic appointee who favored Republican district judges is not partisan:

Partisanship = sum over t of share(t) *
    ((DeferentialReversal(other party, t) - DeferentialReversal(own party, t))
     - (NondeferentialReversal(other party, t) - NondeferentialReversal(own party, t)))

Independence is how often a judge provoked disagreements (dissents and separate concurrences, by the judge or by a copanelist against the judge's opinion) beyond what ideological differences predict. The expected rates are the fitted values of a linear regression, across the judges scored, of the rates on how far each judge's ideology is from the mean of the judge's circuit:

Independence = DissentRate + ConcurrenceRate
    - ExpectedDissentRate - ExpectedConcurrenceRate

A concurrence in part and dissent in part counts as a dissent only.

The adjustments:

  • Case mix. Every rate is computed separately for criminal and civil cases and weighted by the average judge's shares (share(t)). When a judge has too few votes in a cell (fewer than cell_minimum), the judge's rate in both kinds of cases is used, and else the rate of all judges, which is how the studies "interpolated" thin cells.
  • Super-panel effects. The parties of a judge's copanelists and of the district judge change how the judge votes. Each vote's super-panel is one of six alignments ("RR-R", "RR-D", "DR-R", "DR-D", "DD-R", and "DD-D"). The score that a blank-slate judge would have from the alignments that the judge happened to sit in (computed with the rates of all judges in each alignment, so that offsetting alignments cancel) is subtracted.
  • Circuit. Judges who sat in more than one circuit are assumed to keep their traits, so how their scores differ from circuit to circuit measures the circuits. For each circuit, the traveling judges' votes there are scored together, as one hypothetical judge, and compared with their overall scores weighted by their votes there. The difference is the circuit's differential, which is subtracted from the judges of the circuit: divided by twice the number of judges of the circuit ("per judge", as the 2010 and 2011 articles did) or by the number of traveling votes in the circuit and multiplied by the judge's votes there ("per vote", as the 2012 and 2013 articles did). "full" subtracts the whole differential, weighted by the judge's votes in each circuit, which is not in the articles.
  • Scale. The judges with at least minimum interactions with other judges (two copanelists and a district judge on each vote; the studies required 200) define the scale. Activism, partisanship, and independence run from 0 to 100, and ideology from -100 (liberal) to 100 (conservative). Independence is placed on a logarithmic scale first.

The 2013 article revised the earlier methods. method = "typology" (the default) follows it, and method = "original" follows each score's first article:

Choice "original" "typology" Panel and District Scores Added (2010). Weighted by the rate of disagreement at each level. Zero of the Ideology Score The judge whose rank is the number of Democratic appointees (2010). Equal agreement with both parties (no shift). Super-panel effects Ideology and partisanship. Ideology, activism, and partisanship. Circuit adjustment Per judge for ideology and activism (2010, 2011), per vote for partisanship (2012). Per vote for all three. Independence's expected rates From the scaled Ideology Score (2012). From the adjusted raw Ideology Score.

Independence has no circuit adjustment in either, because judges seldom write separately when they travel.

Contents

Methods

the versions of the methods. SCORES: the names of the four scores. score_judges: returns the four scores of every judge in a table of votes.
